15.0.0.en: 1 A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger. 2 The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright: but the mouth of fools poureth out foolishness.

15.0.1.en: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" [1]

15.0.2.en: Many have turned from friends into enemies for long years because of hurtful words, while some have won their enemies and made them their friends by gentle, tender words.

15.0.3.en: Under the cover of defending the truth, or under the cover of frankness and love, we often wound the feelings of our brethren with harsh and violent words. In the Lord Christ's rebuke of the sinful woman He said: "Hath no man condemned thee?... Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more" (Jn 8:10-11). And in His dialogue with the Samaritan woman, He gently asked her to give Him to drink, as one in need of her (Jn 4:7), and when she answered Him: "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria?" - because the Jews do not deal with the Samaritans - He did not wound her feelings with a single word, although He knew her shameful past and her unseemly present. By His gentleness He won her, and indeed won the whole city of Sychar.

15.0.4.en: * The mouth of the chaste speaks good things, delights its owner, and gladdens those who hear. Whoever's speech is orderly and chaste, and who is pure in heart, is a son of Christ's inheritance; but whoever's speech is anxious and clouded with anger is a second devil.

15.0.5.en: * The mouth of the fool overflows with bitterness, kills its owner, and makes drunk those who listen to him.

15.0.6.en: * He who softens his speech and schemes in order to harm is a second devil.

15.0.7.en: The Spiritual Elder * Our Lord offered most of His help by persuasion rather than by blame. Gentle rains soften the earth and seep into it completely, while heavy rain makes it hard and ruins the surface of the ground, so that it does not absorb the water. "Grievous words stir up anger" and with it harm occurs. While the harsh word opens the door, anger enters, and on the heels of anger the harm is done.

15.0.8.en: St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * He who cannot control his tongue at the time of anger will not be able to overcome even the smallest of the passions.

15.0.9.en: Father Irais * "Anger destroys even the prudent, and a soft answer turneth away wrath, and a grievous word stirs up anger"; everything depends on your decision, whether to stir up anger or to walk quietly... And if anger destroys even the prudent, how much more does it destroy those of whom it is said that this anger kills the fool? This happens, without doubt, to the prudent because of neglect. But a soft answer turneth away wrath, that is, an answer given with evident humility, without rudeness.

15.1.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright: but the mouth of fools poureth out foolishness" [2]

15.1.1.en: The tongue is the door of the heart, so the wise man brings forth words of knowledge for his own edification and the edification of his brethren, while the fool brings forth words of folly that corrupt his life and the life of his brethren.

15.1.2.en: The wise man knows what to say, and when, and to what extent; every word has its own weight, and he thinks about it before he utters it.

15.1.3.en: One of the most wonderful examples is the answer of Gideon, full of wisdom and humility, when the men of Ephraim contended with him sharply because he had not called them when he went to fight the Midianites; he said to them: "What have I done now in comparison of you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer? God hath delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, the raven and the wolf: and what was I able to do in comparison of you?" (Judg 8:2-3). And the writer comments: "Then their anger was abated toward him, when he had said that." On the contrary, when the men of Ephraim took the same attitude toward Jephthah when he fought the children of Ammon, instead of answering in a spirit of humility he rebuked them and entered into war with them, in which forty and two thousand of Ephraim were slain (Judg 12:1-6).

15.1.4.en: * He who fasts with his mouth from food but does not fast with his heart from rancor and his tongue from vanities, his fast is in vain, for the fast of the tongue is better than the fast of the mouth, and the fast of the heart is better than the fast of the two. The strength of the body is in foods, and the nourishment of the soul is in speech and tales; and just as the greed for many tales is a desire of the soul, so silence is the fruit of impending wisdom. He who removes from his conscience the faults of his neighbor sows peace in his heart. The simple man who is wise toward God is better than the clever man who is deceitful in his conscience. He who has enslaved his belly and his tongue is better than he who has enslaved the lion, and he who has suppressed the word in his heart is better than he who buried his talent in the earth. The man who is stripped of goodness and yet argues about the virtues is no different from the blind man stripped of light who argues about precious stones and the many colors.

15.2.s.en: 2. Concern to please God, not men

15.2.0.en: "The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good" [3].

15.2.1.en: As the wise man invites us to gentle and soft speech so that we may turn away the spirit of anger from him who troubles us, he also declares that our words are the expression of the wisdom and true knowledge in our hearts and thoughts, for what truly concerns us is to please God, not men. With sweet words our depths must be holy, in harmony with the sweetness of the words. For the eyes of the Lord look into our depths.

15.2.2.en: When Potiphar's wife wanted to draw the young Joseph into sin, he said to her: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Gen 39:9). In the midst of all the harsh circumstances in which he lived, deprived of his parents and sold as a slave, and with his mistress tempting him, he was aware that the eyes of God were watching him!

15.2.3.en: Moses the prophet erred when "he looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man, he slew the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand" (Ex 2:12). He did not look up to realize that God saw him! It is fitting for us in all our conduct, even in our worship, to be occupied with God's looking into our hearts and our inner feelings!

15.2.4.en: * When we gather with the brethren in one place and celebrate the divine sacrifice with the priest of God, we must keep in mind humility and good manners, and not hurl our prayers at random with rude voices nor cast our petitions with violent babbling. Rather, our petition must be offered to God in humility, for God hears our hearts, not our voices.

15.2.5.en: God, who sees our thoughts, is not reproached by shouts, and as the Lord says: [Why think ye vain things in your hearts?] (cf. Mt 9:4). And in another place He says: [All the churches shall know that I am He who searches the desires and the hearts] (cf. Rev 2:23).

15.3.0.en: "A wholesome (calm, sound, healthy) tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a crushing of the spirit" [4]

15.3.1.en: From time to time the wise man returns to speak of the tongue, realizing its gravity, for in its wholesomeness the believer enjoys, as it were, the tree of life, and in its perverseness he loses his life, as his spirit is crushed and murmurs! The tongue can be a blessing that carries a man to the enjoyment of eternal life, and it can be a curse that drives him to eternal punishment.

15.3.2.en: The sound, healthy tongue is the tongue that makes peace among brethren, while the sick, perverse tongue is the one that makes disputes and divisions among brethren. Abraham says to his nephew Lot: "Let there be no strife... for we be brethren" (Gen 13:8).

15.3.3.en: * "A wholesome tongue is a tree of life." The tongue that does not sin in speech is marked by health, for the sickness of the tongue is its sin. He who can control his tongue and not sin is filled with the Holy Spirit.

15.3.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * Be master of your heart and bridle your tongue (Jas 1:26). Take no pleasure in hearing a word against anyone, so that you may have peace with all men, for all the saints of the Lord are in peace, and God dwells in them. As it is written: "Great peace have they which love thy law" (Ps 119:165). Those who love God live in peace with all men.

15.3.5.en: St. Stephen of Thebes * The monk who does not sin with his tongue is truly a shining star on this earth.

15.4.0.en: "A fool despiseth his father's instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is prudent" [5]

15.4.1.en: It is folly for a man to refuse in pride to benefit from the experience of those who have gone before him on the way, whether his parents or his spiritual father.

15.4.2.en: The man who is careful about the salvation of his soul accepts the rebuke of those who have gone before him and their disciplines, just as he accepts the disciplines of the Lord Himself as his heavenly Father, who cares for the salvation of his soul and for bringing him into the heavenly glories. Accepting discipline willingly is a strong proof of the love of wisdom, and it approves the believer before God.

15.4.3.en: * True prudence is knowing what you must do and what you must not do. He who acquires it will not hold back from practicing virtuous deeds, and will not be wounded by the deadly arrow of vice. Thus he who understands the words of prudence knows the difference between what is treacherous, built on deceit, and what reminds us of the calm of the better way in which to live our life. This is like the practice of the money-changer, who holds fast what is good and abstains from every appearance of evil (1 Thess 5:21).

15.4.4.en: Grant such prudence to the builder of his house, so that he lays its foundations on the rock, that is, supports it by faith in Christ, and so is not shaken when the winds, the rains and the storms assail it (Mt 7:25). For through this parable the Lord teaches us to remain steadfast when trials blow, whether their source is human or beyond nature. Besides this, He teaches us not to be ignorant of the necessary things, but to provide ourselves with them for the journey of life, and so to await the coming of the Bridegroom with zealous hearts.

15.4.5.en: Prudence is the quality by which all things are accomplished through skillful perseverance, and in the same way cunning is the quality by which evil is committed. For prudence can be added to every activity, and even evils can happen in all matters; therefore the name of prudence denotes two realities (the one who uses reason for good or for evil).

15.4.6.en: Thus he who uses intelligence and skill for the ruin of others is wicked, while he who acts with uprightness and wisdom reveals his goodness; this one acquires the prudence worthy of praise.

15.4.7.en: Listen diligently to the voice of the prudent soul, and you will know that it contains a center in which sound counsel is given for its own benefit and for the benefit of its neighbor, and is worthy of praise. But the prudence that is used to harm one's neighbor deserves condemnation.

15.4.8.en: St. Basil the Great * If we sin, God may raise up our enemies against us to discipline us, and accordingly we must not fight them, but call ourselves to account and educate ourselves. And as long as He has let them loose on us because of our sins, then if we fight them He gives them victory over us, and for this reason He commanded us not to take vengeance on our enemies. Let us accept trials as we accept medicines from the physician so that we may be saved, and as we accept discipline from the father so that we may be refined. Therefore the wise man said: "My son, if thou come to serve the Lord God, stand fast in righteousness and godliness, and prepare thy soul for temptation" (Sir 2:1).

15.4.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * He who quibbles against discipline drives away from himself the fatherly mercies. He who murmurs against trials has them multiplied upon him. He who is not disciplined here and broken by trials is tormented there without mercy.

15.5.0.en: 6 In the house of the righteous is much treasure: but in the revenues of the wicked is trouble. 7 The lips of the wise disperse knowledge: but the heart of the foolish doeth not so.

15.5.1.en: "In the house of the righteous is much treasure: but in the revenues of the wicked is trouble" [6]

15.5.2.en: The house of the righteous man, which is his heart, holds a precious, inestimable treasure, namely the fruit of the Spirit: joy, love, peace, etc. (Gal 5:22), whereas the revenues of the wicked, or what they gain from their evils, are hatred, anxiety, turmoil, etc. This is the sum of their evils!

15.5.3.en: The mark of the righteous is inner joy and the peace that passes understanding, and the mark of the wicked is anxiety and inner turmoil.

15.5.4.en: The treasure of the righteous is the heavenly Bridegroom, Emmanuel, who dwells by faith in our hearts, and the trouble of the wicked is his deprivation of the heavenly Bridegroom.

15.5.5.en: The righteous enjoy hearts that have been turned into wedding houses for the heavenly Bridegroom, and the hearts of the wicked are turned into a hell in which the evil enemy dwells.

15.5.6.en: * The letter "Eta" means "El" in the Hebrew language אֵל, which means "God", for the prophet Isaiah said "Emmanuel" (Isa 7:14), and St. Matthew the Evangelist, the preacher of the joy that cannot be uttered, interpreted it by saying: "Emmanu" means "with us", and "El" means "God" (Mt 1:23).

15.5.7.en: Let us examine ourselves, then, to see whether God is truly with us. If we are far from evils, and strangers to Satan, who is their source, God is truly with us.

15.5.8.en: If the desire for good works reigns over us and we delight in them, being accustomed to consider our conduct to be in the heavenly places (see Phil 3:20), God is truly with us.

15.5.9.en: If we regard all men as equal and all days as alike, God is truly with us.

15.5.10.en: If we love those who hate us, those who insult us, those who are harsh to us, those who despise us, those who mistreat us and those who trouble us, just as we love those who love us, those who praise us, those who do good to us and give us rest, God is truly with us.

15.5.11.en: And the sign that a man has reached this degree of perfection is his sense that God is always with him - and He is indeed always with him - and his feeling that he has obtained all this.

15.5.12.en: Let him rejoice in the Lord who has understood this, and who will understand it, and who has hope of understanding it!

15.5.13.en: "Eta" means "guide," and the guide is the one who leads.

15.5.14.en: He leads you to the light, so do not seek the darkness.

15.5.15.en: He leads you to uprightness, so do not seek falsehood.

15.5.16.en: He leads you to the truth, so that illusion does not deceive you.

15.5.17.en: He leads you to peace, so do not seek strife.

15.5.18.en: He leads you to joy, so do not strive for sorrow.

15.5.19.en: He leads you to humility, so do not yield to pride.

15.5.20.en: He leads you to justice, so do not look for injustice.

15.5.21.en: He leads you to help you bear the insults and humiliations directed against you, so do not seek praise and vainglory.

15.5.22.en: He leads you to mortification, so do not seek ease and comfort.

15.5.23.en: He leads you to the right side, so do not place yourself among those on the left.

15.5.24.en: He leads you to eternal life, so do not seek eternal punishment in Gehenna, the fire that is not quenched.

15.5.25.en: And the sign of a man's rejecting what ought to be rejected is in his choosing good things, and in never making light of the prayers of the day and the night. Let him rejoice in the Lord who has understood this, and who will understand it, and who has hope of understanding it!

15.6.0.en: St. Barsanuphius "The lips of the wise disperse knowledge: but the heart of the foolish doeth not so" [7]

15.6.1.en: The lips of the wise declare the true knowledge in their hearts, which builds up souls and spreads blessing upon the hearers. But the wicked fools utter the folly in their hearts, which profits no one if it does not harm them.

15.6.2.en: In Paphos Paul and Barnabas spoke with the governor, who sought to hear the word of God (Acts 13:7), but Elymas the sorcerer wanted by his words to turn the governor away from the faith (Acts 13:8).

15.7.0.en: 8 The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD: but the prayer of the upright is his delight. 9 The way of the wicked is an abomination unto the LORD: but he loveth him that followeth after righteousness. 10 Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way: and he that hateth reproof shall die. 11 Hell and destruction are before the LORD: how much more then the hearts of the children of men?

15.7.1.en: "The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD: but the prayer of the upright is his delight" [8]

15.7.2.en: Since God seeks purity of heart, He accepts the prayer of the righteous and delights in it, and rejects the sacrifices and offerings of the wicked. God has no need of our offerings, our sacrifices and our worship; He seeks our hearts.

15.7.3.en: * God has no need of sacrifices, as is very clear in the Holy Scriptures. "I said to the Lord: You are my God, You have no need of my goods" (cf. Ps 16:2), for in accepting or rejecting them He looks only to man's good. God gains no benefit from our worship; rather, we are the ones who gain it.

15.7.4.en: St. Augustine * Cain did not begin his wickedness when he killed his brother. For even before that, God, who knows the heart, did not look upon Cain or upon his sacrifice. His baseness only appeared plainly when he killed Abel.

15.7.5.en: Origen * First of all, God accepted Abel's offering because of the purity of his heart, and Cain's offering was rejected (Gen 4:4). How do we know that Abel's offering was accepted while Cain's offering was rejected? And how did Abel sense that his offering was accepted? And how was Cain assured that his offering was rejected? I will try, as far as I am able, to explain this.

15.7.6.en: You know, my dear one, that the sign of an offering accepted by God is the descent of fire from heaven and the burning of the offering. When Abel and Cain offered their offerings together, the living fire that ministers before God (Ps 104:4) came down and consumed Abel's pure sacrifice, while it did not touch Cain's impure sacrifice. So Abel knew that his offering was accepted, and Cain that his offering was rejected. The fruits of Cain's heart were known afterward, when he was tested and his heart was found full of deceit, when he killed his brother; thus what he conceived in his mind his hands brought forth. But the purity of Abel's heart was the foundation of his prayer.

15.7.7.en: The beloved prayer is the pure prayer, free from all deceit. And prayer is powerful when the power of God works in it.

15.7.8.en: My dear one, I have written to you that when a man commits himself to fulfilling the will of God, and it is the main axis of his prayer, the man is exalted in his prayer. I have told you this so that you do not neglect prayer.

15.7.9.en: St. Aphrahat * We can discover many counsels about other matters also, such as prayer. The Scripture says: Good works are a prayer acceptable to the Lord. The way to prayer is described: if you see a naked man, to clothe him, and not to hide yourself from the members of your household. Then your light shall break forth like the morning, and your garments shall shine speedily, your righteousness shall go before you, and the glory of the Lord shall surround you (cf. Isa 58:7-8).

15.8.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria "The way of the wicked is an abomination unto the LORD: but he loveth him that followeth after righteousness" [9]

15.8.1.en: It is God's delight that man enjoy sonship to Him, and walk as a son of God, according to the Spirit and not according to the flesh. "Because the carnal mind is enmity against God... So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God" (Rom 8:7-8). As was said before, the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord, because their hearts are evil and their ways are evil. It is not fitting for the sinner to offer anything to God unless he offers repentance, that is, returns to God with his heart, and his soul bows in obedience to Him, longing to enjoy His face. So when sinners are justified before the Lord through repentance, and find their delight in Him, and seek Him sincerely, He too delights in their ways, their worship and their spiritual sacrifices.

15.8.2.en: It is as though God seeks man's heart and the renewal of his inner man and his enjoyment of the work of His Holy Spirit, and then he becomes, wholly, the object of God's delight. Thus the believer can chant with sincerity and assurance: "I will go into thy house with burnt offerings: I will pay thee my vows, which my lips have uttered, and my mouth hath spoken, when I was in trouble. I will offer unto thee burnt sacrifices of fatlings, with the incense of rams; I will offer bullocks with goats" (Ps 66:13-15). As he also says: "If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me: but verily God hath heard me; he hath attended to the voice of my prayer" (Ps 66:18-19).

15.8.3.en: * It is clear that the sacrifices were not instituted for their own sake, but to suggest the rest of their way of conduct. When they neglected their principal obligations and busied themselves with nothing but sacrifices, God told them that He would no longer accept them (Amos 5:22; Jer 6:20; Mic 6:6-8).

15.8.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * God Himself says that He requires obedience to His commandments rather than the offering of a sacrifice to Him. God declares this, and Moses declared it to the people of Israel, and Paul preaches it to the Gentiles. Do what you see to be better... "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice" (Mt 9:13).

15.8.5.en: St. Ambrose * The knowledge of God is better than offering sacrifices and burnt offerings, for it brings us to perfection in Christ. For through Him and in Him we know the Father, and become rich in justification by faith.

15.9.0.en: St. Cyril the Great "Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way: and he that hateth reproof shall die" [10]

15.9.1.en: Some translate it: "Discipline (correction) is dangerous for him who leaves the way," like Ahab, who hated whoever gave him honest advice or told him of his error. Ahab said to Jehoshaphat: "There is yet one man, by whom we may enquire of the LORD: but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil. The same is Micaiah the son of Imlah" (1 Kgs 22:8), and also when he met Elijah he said to him: "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?" (1 Kgs 21:20), as he also said to him: "Art thou he that troubleth Israel?" (1 Kgs 18:17). Such also was the attitude of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, who, when he heard part of what was in the scroll, "cut it with the penknife of the scribe, and cast it into the fire that was in the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth" (Jer 36:23). Such kings as these cannot bear the word of God, do not receive men of God, and do not value repentance, but hate the word of truth and honest guidance. Since these hate discipline, they die in their sins.

15.10.0.en: "Hell and destruction are before the LORD: how much more then the hearts of the children of men?" [11]

15.10.1.en: In verse 3 the wise man says that the eyes of the Lord keep watch on the evil and the good in every place. Here he affirms that God, the true Light, sees everything, even hell and destruction, where the height of the darkness of death and ruin is; they are before Him and not hidden from Him, so would anything that is in the hearts of men be hidden from Him? As the Apostle says: "All things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do" (Heb 4:13).

15.10.2.en: What seems invisible to many men, such as heaven, Paradise, Gehenna and hades, are realities seen by God, which He presents to His children by His Holy Spirit, so that they do not see them as imagination, as others think, but see them as facts, and long with all their hearts to cross over into Paradise, to enter heaven, and to be saved from the powers of darkness.

15.10.3.en: The Lord Christ promised us that His Holy Spirit takes of what is His and gives it to us (Jn 16:15), that is, takes of what is visible to Him and declares it to us, so that we even experience the life of Paradise and taste the earnest of the heavenly things, and do not fear hades, for we have no place in it.

15.10.4.en: * Let us marvel to what height He has lifted the Church! He lifted her as by a certain device and set her on high, and seated her on a lofty throne, for where the Head is, there the body is also. There is no separation between them, otherwise the body would no longer be a body, nor the Head a head.

15.10.5.en: * It is possible for us - if we wish - not to be in the body, nor on the earth, but to be in the Spirit, in heaven.

15.10.6.en: Let us enter into our souls... into heaven, in the Spirit!

15.10.7.en: Let us remain in the peace and grace of God, and be freed from fleshly things, and so enjoy good things in Christ our Lord.

15.10.8.en: * It is fitting for you, as you go out from this place, to proclaim that it is a holy place. You go out as men coming down from heaven itself, full of dignity and wisdom, speaking and doing everything with propriety...

15.10.9.en: Teach those outside that you are in the company of the Seraphim.

15.10.10.en: Teach them that you are numbered with the heavenly beings, counted in the ranks of the angels, speaking with the Lord, and in the company of the Lord Christ.

15.10.11.en: And as they look at the beauty of your shining souls, their hearts will be kindled by your good appearance, however dull they may be, for if the beauty of the body entices the one who sees it, how much more does the beauty of the soul and its harmony stir those who behold it and draw them to the same zeal?!

15.10.12.en: * The Church is higher than heaven and wider than the world.

15.11.s.en: 7. The hatred of scorners for him

15.11.0.en: "A scorner loveth not one that reproveth him:

15.11.1.en: neither will he go unto the wise." [12]

15.11.2.en: By this proverb he makes clearer still what was stated in (verse 10). The unserious person, the scorner, cares nothing for the things of the world to come, even though they are firm realities seen before the Lord. What occupies him is his pleasures and his honor, so he hates the one who reproves him, and does not wish to sit with the wise and speak with them. He counts their talk about eternity as imagination, a waste of time and a deprivation of pleasures.

15.12.0.en: 13 A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken. 14 The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge: but the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness. 15 All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.

15.12.1.en: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken" [13]

15.12.2.en: Divine consolations fill the heart of the spiritual man, and reflect on his face a constant cheerfulness, able to face tribulations.

15.12.3.en: The spiritual man sees his Christ dwelling in his heart, satisfying him, guiding his life and delivering him from tribulations, and even turning sufferings into glories, as they become a fellowship of sufferings with Him.

15.12.4.en: Nothing breaks a man like hidden inner sorrow, and his failure to realize the truth of the work of the Lord Christ as his Savior from sins and the bearer of his burdens.

15.12.5.en: * This joy is not separated from sorrow, for rather it clings to us in a deep way. He who grieves over his errors and confesses them rejoices. Instead of sorrow over sins, joy in Christ is realized... Therefore he says: "Rejoice in the Lord" (Phil 4:4). For this (sorrow) becomes as nothing with the acceptance of a life made worthy of joy.

15.12.6.en: St. John Chrysostom In (the Long Rules), Question 17 concerned laughter, and St. Basil the Great made clear the necessity of distinguishing between corrupting laughter and laughter in the sense of the soul's joy and exultation in God.

15.12.7.en: * Those who live under discipline (self-control of the soul) must avoid even such an excessive activity with all care, so that it is used lightly. For indulging in laughter in an uncontrolled and exaggerated way is a sign of excess and a lack of control of one's feelings, and a failure to suppress the frivolity of the soul by using reason firmly. It is not unseemly to bear witness to the merriment of the soul with a cheerful smile, if only it illustrates what is written: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance" (Prov 15:13). But coarse laughter, without control of the movements of the body, is not an indication of a soul that has a good, moderate management, or of personal dignity, or of one who rules over himself.

15.12.8.en: This kind of laughter the Preacher condemns especially as destroying the steadiness of the soul, in the words: "I said of laughter, It is error (madness)" (Eccl 2:2). Again: "For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool" (Eccl 7:6). Moreover, the Lord shows that He experienced these necessary emotions that belong to the body, as well as those connected with virtue, for example sorrowing with the sorrowful and compassion for them, but as we know from the story of the Gospel, He never laughed. On the contrary, He declared that those who give themselves over to laughter are unhappy (Lk 6:25).

15.12.9.en: Let us not allow the word (laughter) to deceive us, for it has two meanings.

15.12.10.en: For the Holy Scriptures often use it of the joy of the Spirit and the gladness of the feelings that follows good works. For example, Sarah says: "God hath made me to laugh" (Gen 21:6). And there is another saying: "Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh" (Lk 6:21). In a similar way the words of Job: "Till he fill thy mouth with laughing" (Job 8:21). All these witnesses to gladness point to the merriment of the soul rather than boisterous merriment. Therefore he who is master of every passion and feels no agitation in his pleasure, or at least shows no outward expressions, but tends to restrain firmly every harmful pleasure, such a one is perfectly chaste, and is in the same truth plainly free from every sin...

15.12.11.en: If a man flees from all the provocations of sin but falls prey to even one of them, such a man is not chaste. Like one who is not sound in health when he suffers from one single illness. And like one who is not considered a free man if he falls under the authority of any person, regardless of who that person is.

15.13.0.en: St. Basil the Great "The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge: but the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness" [14]

15.13.1.en: The heart of the man of understanding does not exalt itself over his understanding and knowledge, but thirsts for new depths of knowledge, so he remains always looking at himself as one who looks in a mirror, in a riddle, until he meets the Lord Christ - the Wisdom of God - face to face. His thirst for knowledge and his constant hunger for the truth give him humility along with earnestness and a striving to enjoy new heavenly, divine experiences.

15.13.2.en: But the mouth of fools overflows with the amusement, jesting and indifference to eternity that are in their hearts, so their words come forth as a pasture of folly, satisfying no one's heart and supporting no one.

15.14.0.en: "All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast" [15]

15.14.1.en: He who does not experience the sweetness of salvation has sorrow take possession of his heart, and is captive to gloom, so he lives in misery and wretchedness; but he who tastes the sweetness of fellowship with the Lord Christ has his heart turned into a joyful wedding feast. He rejoices and makes his brethren rejoice with him, as the Lord delights in him, and the heavenly hosts exult in his salvation.

15.14.2.en: * "Rejoice in the Lord alway" (Phil 4:4). This means that the result of unity in understanding and faith is that they rejoice in the Lord, and that each of them is dear to the others. He says: "Rejoice in the Lord" - this is very little - "and again I say, Rejoice." For when you are united together in heart you rejoice in the Lord, and when you rejoice in the Lord you are united in heart and stand in the Lord.

15.15.0.en: 16 Better is little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble therewith. 17 Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.

15.15.1.en: "Better is little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble therewith" [16]

15.15.2.en: Here he sets up a contrast between the fear of the Lord and trouble, as though the fear of the Lord were bound up with true inner surrender and reliance on the Almighty and the enjoyment of inner peace. And deprivation of the divine fear makes a man lose his peace, even if he enjoys treasures of such measure.

15.15.3.en: There is no basis for comparison between Daniel the captive, without resources, and the company of the wise men and sorcerers, counselors of the greatest king of that time. The first acquired the fear of the Lord, so he refused to eat of the king's delicacies offered to the idols, not for the sake of his bodily health (a diet), but for the fear of the Lord, and he became the second man after the greatest king of that age, whereas the wise men were nearly put to death had not the prophet Daniel rescued them by interpreting the king's dream.

15.16.0.en: "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith" [17]

15.16.1.en: * This is a reminder of what we said before, that vegetables are not agape (`agapy`) in themselves, but meals must be practiced with love. The middle way is the good way in everything, and especially at banquets. Excesses are in fact dangerous; humility is good, and whatever avoids pressing need is humble. Natural desires have their limits in inner satisfaction.

15.16.2.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith" (Prov 15:17). We often prefer simple, economical hospitality from hosts who receive us with a good conscience - but who have not the means to offer more - to those who, with arrogant words lifted up against the knowledge of God (2 Cor 10:5), seduce us to learn something foreign to the Father of our Lord Jesus (Mt 5:17).

15.16.3.en: Origen * Be content with what you have, and do not allow your condition to be improved by harming your neighbor. You will find your way of living in the simplicity of innocence. He who has his own goodness knows nothing of laying an ambush for others. He is not inflamed with the desire of the covetous man, who gains his profit at the expense of virtue and out of greed. Therefore he must recognize his blessings, and so the poor man becomes truly happy, since he lives in righteousness in a way better than all the treasures of the world, for "better is little with the fear of the Lord than all great treasures without fear"... May we use our talents to seek grace and obtain salvation, and not to deceive others who have done us no harm at all.

15.16.4.en: * When someone invites hungry guests to dinner who have a ready appetite for eating, then even if he sets a humble table it appears plentiful in the eyes of the guests, who fall upon the dishes with great desire. In the same way, with regard to your spiritual appetite, do not hold back if we set before you a poor and lowly table, offered in an ordinary way before your goodness.

15.16.5.en: This is also what a wise man observed when he said: "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith" (Prov 15:17), suggesting that love gives a different point of view, so that ordinary things appear rich in its eyes, and scraps appear as nobility and generosity.

15.16.6.en: St. Basil the Great * Good is hospitality with vegetables. I will make clear what (Solomon) says. For the one who fears the Lord and delights in the benefits of men, it is better to have little than to have much. Truly, delight is not in abundance (of goods), but rather abundance is in delight.

15.17.0.en: "A wrathful man stirreth up strife: but he that is slow to anger appeaseth strife" [18]

15.17.1.en: Haste in anger is the natural fruit of pride, for the proud man cannot bear anyone who wounds his feelings with an insult, or with what seems to him a robbing of his rights, so the fires of anger are kindled in him and it is hard for him to quench them, and anger turns into strife and agitation. But the humble man longs to win every soul whatever the cost, and if a quarrel arises he soothes it through gentle speech.

15.17.2.en: When the anger of King Saul was kindled against David he tried to kill him, and he could not bear his son Jonathan's defense of David, so that he hurled the spear at him to smite him (1 Sam 20:33). Saul was determined to kill David, but when Saul fell into David's hand he did not touch him, but cut off the skirt of Saul's robe, and he could not bear even that, since his heart smote him for it. And gently he called after Saul, and stooped with his face to the earth, and bowed himself (1 Sam 24:8). And he said: "Behold, this day thine eyes have seen how that the LORD had delivered thee today into mine hand in the cave: and some bade me kill thee: but mine eye spared thee; and I said, I will not put forth mine hand against my lord; for he is the LORD'S anointed" (1 Sam 24:10). Saul lifted up his voice and wept, and said to David: "Thou art more righteous than I... the LORD reward thee good for that thou hast done unto me this day."

15.18.0.en: "The way of the slothful man is as an hedge of thorns: but the way of the upright is a highway" [19]

15.18.1.en: While the sluggard thinks that he rests by not working, behold, a hedge of thorns grows up within him as well as around him, so he finds no peace in his depths. But he who walks uprightly and diligently, with all the opposition he meets, finds his way made smooth. Troubles are turned to work on his behalf.

15.18.2.en: The first, with every slackness, finds all matters in his life becoming entangled, so his life becomes a chain of weariness that comes upon him. The second, since he knows the way and perceives his goal in life, goes up from step to step. And if he stumbles on the way, he rises with greater strength in joyful hope.

15.18.3.en: Since David did not know laziness, he sang, saying: "For by thee I have run through a troop; and by my God have I leaped over a wall" (Ps 18:29).

15.18.4.en: * When they turn aside from the royal road they are unable to reach the city to which we must come on our journey, and they lose their direction. The Preacher says: "The labour of the foolish wearieth every one of them, because he knoweth not how to go to the city" (Eccl 10:15)... I mean the heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of us all (Gal 4:26).

15.18.5.en: St. John Cassian * There are those who are called lazy in the Book of Wisdom, who cover their way with thorns, and count zeal in keeping the commandments of God as harmful to the soul, who object to the apostolic commandments, who do not eat their bread by toil but go around to others, and make idleness the rule of life. Then there are the dreamers, who count the deceptions of dreams more trustworthy than the teachings of the Gospels, and call fantasies revelations. Besides these there are also those who dwell in their houses, whom others consider unsociable and wild, not knowing the commandment of love and not knowing the fruit of longsuffering and humility.

15.19.0.en: "A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish man despiseth his mother" [20]

15.19.1.en: This proverb came similar to what is in (Proverbs 10:1).

15.19.2.en: And as was said before, the wise son refers to the believer in whom his heavenly Father rejoices, and receives him as an heir of the Father, an heir with Christ. But the foolish man, who relies on his own opinions in arrogance, despises the Church his mother, counting himself wiser, more understanding and more spiritual than the Church.

15.20.0.en: 21 Folly is joy to him that is destitute of wisdom: but a man of understanding walketh uprightly. 22 Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.

15.20.1.en: "Folly is joy to him that is destitute of wisdom: but a man of understanding walketh uprightly" [21]

15.20.2.en: The foolish man, lacking understanding, finds his delight in evil and in his irresponsible, foolish conduct, but the man of understanding walks uprightly in the fear of the Lord, and rejects wicked pleasures, amusement and jesting.

15.21.0.en: "Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established" [22]

15.21.1.en: The wise man does not rely on his own opinion alone in important matters, but listens to those who have knowledge and experience. Perhaps for this reason the Lord sent His disciples and apostles two by two, that they might take counsel together, and share in preaching and worship.

15.22.0.en: 23 A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it! 24 The way of life is above to the wise, that he may depart from hell beneath.

15.22.1.en: "A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it!" [23]

15.22.2.en: A fitting answer at the right time, in a fitting manner, and within sound limits gladdens the heart of the speaker and the heart of the listener, and leaves no room for a man to regret what he has said.

15.22.3.en: Here he stresses the manner of answering and the choice of the right time. For a sound answer at the wrong time may do more harm than silence and not answering. And also a wrong answer at the right time may cause a disaster!

15.23.0.en: "The way of life is above to the wise, that he may depart from hell beneath" [24]

15.23.1.en: Since the wise man enjoys true life, he lives always in ascents, rising from glory to glory (2 Cor 3:18), and at the same time avoids descending downward into hell.

15.23.2.en: Life knows no standing still: it is either ascent toward the heavenly things or descent toward hell. Some compare it to one who swims in the middle of a river: either he completes his course to cross to the shore, or he stops swimming and drowns.

15.23.3.en: Before man are two ways: the way of life, which knows no idleness, or the way of death.

15.23.4.en: * He who pursues perfection, clings to the ascent to heaven, and looks to the path on high cannot rest and stop at one height, thinking that he is complete in his work and no longer needs to ascend to another step, but he hastens daily to rise higher, until death opens the door for him to reach the harbor of the saints. I say to you, lover of virtues, it is good for you to think and meditate about advancing forward. And it is fitting for you to reckon that there is a greater way of life than yours. If you thought that you had climbed by virtue as far as you should have climbed, your striving would be in vain, and you would begin to descend because of the pretension that steals over your soul, and fall from the beauty of humility.

15.23.5.en: * I cry out with all my strength: if you find a place farther than yourself, flee to it, and if you find a place within you, withdraw to it. Do not cease to flee, and do not rest from running until you attain that for which Christ attained you (Phil 3:13).

15.23.6.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh * Growth takes place gradually from childhood to maturity and perfection in Christ. For faith increases and grows by the work of the divine Holy Spirit. Accordingly, the strongholds of evil thoughts are gradually broken until they are entirely demolished.

15.24.0.en: 25 The LORD will destroy the house of the proud: but he will establish the border of the widow. 26 The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD: but the words of the pure are pleasant words. 27 He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live.
